csis_directors.name: Richard Fadden
csis_directors.role: Director of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service
csis_directors.notable: Director 2009-2013. Public CBC interview June 2010 flagged provincial cabinet members as subjects of foreign influence — precedent-setting public statement on foreign interference from a sitting CSIS Director. Transitioned to National Security Advisor then Deputy Minister of Defence.

csis_directors.name: Michel Coulombe
csis_directors.role: Director of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service
csis_directors.notable: Director 2013-2017. Led CSIS through the Bill C-51 Anti-terrorism Act 2015 expansion of 'threat reduction measures' (CSIS disruption powers) — the largest statutory expansion of CSIS authority since 1984. Testified before SECU on C-51.

csis_directors.name: David Vigneault
csis_directors.role: Director of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service
csis_directors.notable: Director 2017-2024. Custodian during foreign interference escalation: Global News Nov 2022 reports, Han Dong resignation Mar 2023, Johnston Special Rapporteur May-June 2023, Hogue Commission establishment Sept 2023, and Federal Court 2020 'duty of candour' ruling on CSIS warrant applications. Publicly warned of PRC interference.

csis_directors.name: Daniel Rogers
csis_directors.role: Director of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service
csis_directors.notable: Director from July 2024. Former Associate Chief of Communications Security Establishment. Holds portfolio during Hogue Commission final report (Jan 2025), Bill C-70 Countering Foreign Interference Act implementation, and the ongoing PRC/India interference investigations.

public_safety_ministers.name: Vic Toews
public_safety_ministers.notable: Public Safety Minister during Fadden's public foreign-interference statement and subsequent parliamentary controversy. Oversaw CSIS responsibilities during the post-Arar reform era.

public_safety_ministers.name: Steven Blaney
public_safety_ministers.notable: Minister who tabled and advanced Bill C-51 Anti-terrorism Act 2015. Expanded CSIS threat-reduction measures authority. One of the most consequential ministers for CSIS statutory scope in the modern era.

public_safety_ministers.name: Ralph Goodale
public_safety_ministers.notable: Introduced and passed Bill C-59 National Security Act 2017 — created NSIRA, established Intelligence Commissioner, modified CSIS threat-reduction, re-drew dataset rules. Structural modernisation of the national-security review regime.

public_safety_ministers.name: Marco Mendicino
public_safety_ministers.notable: Minister during Emergencies Act invocation Feb 2022 (Rouleau Commission follow-up), initial foreign-interference disclosures Nov 2022, and the Johnston Special Rapporteur appointment. Fired by PM July 2023 over Paul Bernardo transfer (tracked in Corrections dossier). Cross-axis: Corrections, Foreign dossiers.

public_safety_ministers.name: Dominic LeBlanc
public_safety_ministers.role: Minister of Public Safety (plus Intergovernmental Affairs)
public_safety_ministers.notable: Took portfolio July 2023. Shepherded Bill C-70 Countering Foreign Interference Act (Royal Assent June 2024) and responded to Hogue Commission. Cross-axis: Foreign, Carney, RCMP dossiers (quadruple-spread actor).

nsira_chairs.name: Murray Rankin
nsira_chairs.role: Chair, National Security and Intelligence Review Agency
nsira_chairs.notable: Inaugural NSIRA Chair July 2019 - stood up the agency created by Bill C-59 from the former Security Intelligence Review Committee. Resigned 2020 after election as BC MLA. Short but foundational tenure.

nsira_chairs.name: Marie Deschamps
nsira_chairs.role: Chair (interim then substantive), National Security and Intelligence Review Agency
nsira_chairs.notable: Former SCC Justice. Chaired NSIRA through the CSIS duty-of-candour Federal Court ruling July 2020, the foreign-interference review 2023, and multiple inter-agency information-sharing reviews. Also authored 2015 Deschamps Report into CAF sexual misconduct (cross-axis: CFNIS dossier).

nsicop_chairs.name: David McGuinty
nsicop_chairs.role: Chair, National Security and Intelligence Committee of Parliamentarians
nsicop_chairs.notable: Inaugural NSICOP Chair, Liberal MP Ottawa South. Tabled the June 2024 NSICOP special report on foreign interference in democratic institutions — naming parliamentarians as 'witting or semi-witting' collaborators. The report precipitated demands for names to be disclosed and shaped the Hogue Commission's remaining work.

nsicop_chairs.name: David McGuinty (Minister Public Safety 2024-2025)
nsicop_chairs.role: Minister of Public Safety (moved from NSICOP Chair)
nsicop_chairs.notable: Appointed Minister of Public Safety Dec 2024 (Trudeau cabinet shuffle) after his NSICOP chairmanship - unusual direct move from parliamentary-review body to the minister overseeing CSIS. Continued into Carney government transition. Note: single individual appears twice by role to preserve 16-actor fixed structure.

prime_ministers_of_record.name: Stephen Harper
prime_ministers_of_record.notable: PM during CSIS Act era of expanded authorities culminating in Bill C-51 2015. Appointed Fadden and Coulombe as Directors. Defined the post-9/11 national-security architecture that Bill C-59 would later modify.

prime_ministers_of_record.name: Justin Trudeau
prime_ministers_of_record.notable: PM during C-59 reform, foreign-interference disclosures 2022-2024, Johnston Special Rapporteur appointment, Hogue Commission, and Bill C-70. PMO central to handling classified briefings on interference. Cross-axis: quintuple-Grover-marked (indigenous/rcmp/veterans/judicial/phoenix_pay). Expected to extend to this axis.

prime_ministers_of_record.name: Mark Carney
prime_ministers_of_record.notable: Current PM. Inherits Hogue Commission final-report implementation, Bill C-70 operationalisation, foreign-registry transparency requirements, and ongoing CSIS-RCMP coordination mandates on interference. Cross-axis: Carney-Brookfield, Indigenous, Veterans, Judicial dossiers.

timeline.event: Fadden public CBC interview warns of foreign influence on Canadian officials.
Bill C-51 Anti-terrorism Act receives Royal Assent, granting CSIS threat-reduction powers.
Bill C-59 National Security Act tabled.
NSICOP Act creates National Security and Intelligence Committee of Parliamentarians.
Bill C-59 receives Royal Assent, creating NSIRA and Intelligence Commissioner.
NSIRA stood up, replacing SIRC. Rankin first Chair.
Federal Court ruling 2020 FC 757: CSIS breached duty of candour in warrant applications.
Emergencies Act invoked; CSIS role in assessment becomes focus of Rouleau Commission.
Global News reports CSIS briefings on PRC interference in 2019/2021 elections.
Han Dong resigns from Liberal caucus amid interference allegations.
David Johnston appointed Independent Special Rapporteur on Foreign Interference.
Johnston resigns following non-confidence motion; Hogue Commission announced.
Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference (Hogue Commission) formally established.
NSICOP special report on foreign interference in democratic institutions published, McGuinty chair.
Bill C-70 Countering Foreign Interference Act receives Royal Assent.
Hogue Commission final report released - concludes foreign interference did not change election outcomes but trust damage is real.

statutory_framework: Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act - R.S.C. 1985, c. C-23
National Security Act, 2017 - S.C. 2019, c. 13 (Bill C-59 - created NSIRA + IC)
National Security and Intelligence Committee of Parliamentarians Act - S.C. 2017, c. 15
Countering Foreign Interference Act - S.C. 2024, c. 16 (Bill C-70)
commissions_and_inquiries: Rouleau Commission (Public Order Emergency Commission) 2022-2023 - CSIS role in Emergencies Act
Johnston Special Rapporteur on Foreign Interference 2023 - resigned
Hogue Commission Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference 2023-2025
NSICOP special report on foreign interference 2024
implementation_tracking: Federal Court warrant jurisprudence (duty of candour line)
accountability_chain.result_2025: CSIS statutory scope modernised by C-51 (expanded) then C-59 (checked) then C-70 (countering foreign interference). Federal Court 2020 ruling formally criticised CSIS for duty-of-candour breach. Hogue Commission concluded foreign interference did not change election outcomes but trust damage is real. NSICOP flagged sitting parliamentarians as witting/semi-witting collaborators without public naming. No criminal prosecutions of named parliamentarians. Bill C-70 foreign-influence transparency registry in operationalisation.
